method: For each seed we opened the provider's own documentation, compared the guide's claims to it, and kept the source that matched. Where a page wouldn't open or didn't answer the question, the claim stays inferred or unknown instead of being rounded up.

entries.claim: Which Google page covers verification requirements
entries.detail: Search pointed at support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463816. It turned out to cover only annual recertification. Initial-verification claims were re-sourced from the Unverified apps page and the audience page.

entries.claim: 'Testing mode tokens last 7 days' is the whole story
entries.detail: Google's audience page confirms the 7 days, and adds an exception we would have missed: apps that ask only for openid, email and profile skip the test-user list, the warning and the expiry. That became the first nuance.
The page says 100 new users, counted after the warning screen first appears, for the life of the project, and not resettable. The guide uses that wording.

entries.claim: Google's own review and security-assessment timelines
entries.detail: No Google page we could open states one. The only numbers come from a 2021 vendor article, so the guide labels them 'reported' and says why.

entries.claim: One page covers business verification, App Review and the yearly check-up
entries.detail: The 2023 announcement names only business verification. Review steps and the Data Use Checkup come from the Trust Center page. Sources were split so each claim points at the page that actually says it.

entries.claim: How long business verification and App Review take
entries.detail: Neither Meta page states a timeline. Community reports vary widely and were not treated as evidence. The wait is fogged.

The authorization page says the authorize URL appears after the connection is submitted for review. Notion doesn't say what is reviewed or whether it blocks testing. Downgraded to unknown rather than asserting either way.

entries.claim: Current development-mode limits and extended-quota thresholds
entries.detail: A February 2026 announcement changed developer access. We could read the thread header but not the announcement. The 25-user figure comes from a May 2021 post that says it may be outdated, and the guide says so.

entries.claim: A LinkedIn Page must verify your app
entries.detail: Believed true from practice. LinkedIn's help article refused our fetch, so it stays 'inferred' with a note, not 'sourced'.

entries.claim: One callback URL per OAuth app, no review step mentioned
entries.detail: Matches the creation docs. Caveat: the page we could open was the Enterprise Server 3.8 version, so the guide flags possible drift from github.com.

entries.claim: HTTPS redirect URLs, 10-minute code expiry, bad_redirect_uri with multiple URLs
entries.detail: All three stated on Slack's OAuth page. The Marketplace review timeline is not stated anywhere we read, so it is unknown.

entries.claim: The server count where verification becomes required
entries.detail: The application reference names 100 servers for privileged intents but gives no verification threshold or process. We didn't fill the gap.

limits: No OAuth apps were registered. Doing so means creating accounts and passing identity checks, which an agent shouldn't do for you. What an agent can do here is read, probe public endpoints with dummy credentials, and prepare everything you paste in.

Tested claims come from credential-free probes of each provider's authorize and token endpoints (dummy client, no real credentials), run on 2026-10-29. They show the endpoint answers and how it errors, nothing about approval.
Documentation changes. Every source carries the date we read it; treat anything older than a quarter as a prompt to re-check.
